title: The Second Letter to the Thessalonians
subtitle: Pros Thessalonikeis B, “Second to the Thessalonians”
description: A short letter to a persecuted church thrown into alarm by a claim that the day of the Lord had already come. Paul thanks God for faith that is growing under suffering and promises that God will set things right when the Lord Jesus appears; he insists that the day has not yet arrived, for the great rebellion and the man of lawlessness must come first, held back for now by a power the Thessalonians knew and we do not; and he tells those who have stopped working to earn their own bread, closing with a greeting in his own hand. In the Open Word Bible, a new translation from the Greek given freely to the public domain, with an introduction to the letter’s shape and meaning and a conclusion on where to read next.

qa.question: What is the Second Letter to the Thessalonians about?
qa.answer: It is a short letter to the church in Thessalonica, written to steady believers who were being persecuted and had been told that the day of the Lord had already come. It encourages them that God will judge justly when the Lord Jesus appears (chapter 1), explains that the day cannot have come yet, because the great rebellion and the man of lawlessness must come first (chapter 2), and commands those who had stopped working to go back to work (chapter 3).

qa.question: Who wrote 2 Thessalonians, and when?
qa.answer: The letter names Paul, Silvanus and Timothy as its senders, and Paul signs it in his own hand (3:17). The traditional view, held by many scholars, is that Paul wrote it from Corinth around AD 51, soon after 1 Thessalonians. Many other modern scholars think a follower of Paul wrote it later, because of its close imitation of the first letter and its different emphasis about the end; others answer that a new problem in the church explains the differences.

qa.question: Who is the man of lawlessness in 2 Thessalonians 2?
qa.answer: Paul describes a figure who will set himself against every god, take his seat in God’s temple and present himself as God, before the Lord Jesus destroys him at his coming (2:3–8). Early Christian writers such as Irenaeus and Cyril of Jerusalem identified him with the Antichrist of the last days; the Reformers often saw the papacy; others think of a figure still to come or of a recurring pattern of rebellion against God. Paul says that something is holding him back, which the Thessalonians knew about; Augustine admitted he did not know what it was, and Christians still disagree.

qa.question: Why does 2 Thessalonians say the day of the Lord had not yet come?
qa.answer: Someone, by a prophetic word, a spoken message or a letter claiming to come from Paul, was telling the church that the day of the Lord was already here (2:2). Paul answers that it cannot have come, because certain things must happen first: the great rebellion, and the unveiling of the man of lawlessness, who is being held back for now (2:3–7). The false claim was not that the day was near, which Paul himself taught, but that it had already arrived. His purpose is pastoral. Evil is real but on a leash, and the Lord Jesus will destroy it at his coming, so believers need not be shaken.

qa.question: What does “Anyone who will not work should not eat” mean in 2 Thessalonians 3:10?
qa.answer: Paul repeats a rule he had given the church in person, because some members were living undisciplined lives, not busy working but busy with everyone else’s business, and expecting the church to feed them. The rule is about those who will not work, not those who cannot. Paul points to his own example: he worked night and day so as not to be a burden, though he had a right to support. And he is careful about how the rule is applied. The church is to keep its distance from such a person, but not to treat him as an enemy; he is to be corrected as a brother or sister.

qa.question: Which translation of the Bible is this?
qa.answer: The Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Greek and dedicated to the public domain, printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. The reasoning behind each of its sentences, with the Greek beside it, is published at openwordbible.org. The introduction and conclusion were written for this edition.
